title: Tesla workers balk at training Optimus humanoid robots as replacements
gist: Citing The Information, Tesla's Optimus V3 humanoid ramp is hampered by hand-assembly of 100+ component hands, unreliable touch sensors, task-specific AI, worker resistance to motion-capture data collection, and reliance on Chinese suppliers; Tesla is at hundreds of robots per week versus a 1,000+/week end-2026 target, amid competition from Hyundai/Boston Dynamics, Toyota and Agility.

insights.claim: Tesla stopped making the Model S and Model X at its Fremont factory in May 2026 and moved line workers and engineers to Optimus humanoid robot work, per The Information.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Tesla is committing real manufacturing capacity to Optimus, raising the stakes of execution on Elon Musk's robotics thesis.

insights.claim: Tesla has reportedly scaled Optimus production to hundreds of robots per week but is targeting more than 1,000 per week by the end of 2026, with Optimus V3 facing line-alignment and line-speed problems.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Track weekly Optimus output vs the 1,000/week target as a key credibility test for Tesla's valuation narrative.
insights.locator: But the newest version of Optimus

insights.claim: Elon Musk called Optimus potentially 'the biggest product ever' on Tesla's Q2 2026 earnings call while acknowledging a general-purpose autonomous humanoid is 'one of the hardest things to solve'.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Management hype vs reported execution issues; the author notes Musk frequently makes claims that fail to materialize.
insights.locator: As someone who frequently makes claims

insights.claim: Optimus hands and forearms contain over 100 small components and are manually assembled, producing robots that need immediate fixes, and unreliable hand touch sensors led Tesla to develop a replaceable glove-like sensor layer.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Dexterous hands are the manufacturing bottleneck for humanoids; hand/actuator/tactile-sensor suppliers are a key picks-and-shovels angle.

insights.claim: Optimus's AI is reportedly not yet general-purpose; the robots currently need programming for specific tasks in carefully controlled environments.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: General-purpose humanoid economics remain unproven; near-term deployments look like conventional task-specific automation.

insights.claim: Tesla had factory workers in Texas and California wear motion-capture suits to generate imitation-learning data, but workers complained they were training their replacements, so Tesla shifted collection to dedicated teams and training hubs.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Training-data acquisition is a cost and labor-relations bottleneck for humanoid robotics; dedicated data-collection operations add expense.
insights.quote: knew the robots were designed to eventually replace them

insights.claim: Tesla continues to rely on Chinese suppliers for various Optimus components, even as the FCC in July banned new foreign-made robots including humanoids, robot dogs and robot vacuums.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: US robotics supply chains remain China-dependent; policy pushes create reshoring opportunities and cost risk for US humanoid makers.

insights.claim: Hyundai plans to deploy up to 25,000 Boston Dynamics Atlas humanoids over the next several years, and Toyota plans to invest billions in factory robots including some humanoids.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Automakers in Korea and Japan are credible humanoid competitors to Tesla, with captive factory demand.

insights.claim: Agility Robotics is among the furthest along in commercial humanoid deployment, having put robots to work at a GXO Logistics warehouse near Atlanta in 2024, but the humanoid business case still needs sustained, cost-effective, safe deployments.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Logistics is the early humanoid use case; proof of ROI remains the gating item for the whole sector.
